paper_title: Explicit Style Extraction for Personalized Long-Form Text Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid, then drafts from the user's samples and revises the draft twice against this profile, guided by its own style scores. On the three long-form tasks of LongLaMP with three LLMs, SP-Refine outperforms LongLaMP's retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 ROUGE and METEOR comparisons, by 10.2% on average and by up to 35.8%. Annotating users' own texts with the extracted profiles shows that StylePrism captures concrete, checkable habits, from the order of rhetorical moves to a reviewer's sign-off. Ablations show that the profile helps as revision guidance, not as a replacement for the samples: writing from the profile alone is worse in all 27 comparisons, while a single implicit-inference call is a cheaper alternative that comes close. Oracle variants that let the reviser see the reference, together with reference-free controls, show that larger refinement gains require information unavailable at inference time.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft text on persons behalf: research abstracts, product reviews, social media posts. For 1 such text to be useful, it should be correct and fluent and also sound like its author. Personalized text generation studies this problem by conditioning model on users writing history (Salemi et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024), and the LongLaMP benchmark (Kumar et al., 2024) extends it to longform outputs, where differences in style between users are most visible. The dominant approach is retrieval-augmented personalization: retrieve the users past texts that are most relevant to the current input and place them in the prompt (Salemi et al., 2024b; Kumar et al., 2024; Salemi et al., 2024a). Retrieval decides which samples the model sees, but says little about what the model should take from them. In LongLaMP, the retrieved samples are followed by single instruction such as Following the given patterns. Whether the model attends to sentence rhythm, hedging, discourse moves, or formatting is left implicit. We make style an explicit, inspectable intermediate. STYLEPRISM (Figure 2) organizes writing style into 28 aspects in seven categories, from lexical choice to cross-task fingerprints. SP-REFINE (Algorithm 1) uses it as function: given the retrieved samples, the model first extracts style profile that fills every STYLEPRISM aspect with an observed pattern, quoted evidence, and habits to avoid; it then drafts the output from the samples, and revises the draft twice against the profile, scoring its own revision on five style criteria and fixing the weakest. Unlike retrieval-augmented generation, SP-REFINE produces profile that person can read and check (Figure 3). We evaluate on the three long-form LongLaMP tasks with three LLM families, using referencebased metrics and rubric-based LLM judge that scores style fidelity and task quality separately (Figure 1). Our contributions are: STYLEPRISM, taxonomy of writing style that serves as the schema for extraction, the guide for revision, and the basis of our style rubric. SP-REFINE, which outperforms LongLaMPs retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 reference-based comparisons and improves LLM-judged style fidelity over it in 8 of 9 generatortask settings. An annotation study of users reference texts showing which profile aspects are borne out by what the user actually wrote, and where users depart from their own profile. Ablations and an oracle study showing that the profile works as revision guidance but not as replacement for the samples, and separating gains achievable at inference time from those that need the reference.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Personalized text generation. LaMP (Salemi et al., 2024b) introduced benchmark for personalizing LLM outputs with retrieved user history, and LongLaMP (Kumar et al., 2024) extended it to long-form generation. Most methods follow the retrieval-augmented recipe and improve the retriever (Salemi et al., 2024a; Mysore et al., 2024), summarize the users history (Richardson et al., 2023), or decompose personalization into multiple stages (Li et al., 2023); see Zhang et al. (2024) for survey. We keep retrieval fixed and study what the model is told to extract from the retrieved samples and how it uses it. Representing writing style. Style has been studied in style representation learning, where central difficulty is separating style from content (Wegmann et al., 2022), and in style transfer (Jin et al., 2022). LLMs can transfer style from instructions and few examples (Reif et al., 2022) and describe stylistic attributes in natural language (Patel et al., 2023). STYLEPRISM organizes such attributes into schema that an LLM fills from handful of samples, with quoted evidence for each claim. Refinement and LLM-based evaluation. LLMs can critique and revise their own outputs (Madaan et al., 2023), and LLM judges are widely used to evaluate generation (Zheng et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023), although they can favor their own outputs (Panickssery et al., 2024). SP-REFINEs revisions are guided by an explicit style profile and never see the reference; we compare them with oracle revisions that do.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Data. We use the three public long-form tasks of LongLaMP (Kumar et al., 2024) in the user setting, in which test users do not appear in training: abstract generation (title and key items abstract), review writing (rating, product description, and summary review), and topic writing (Reddit post summary post). We evaluate on the full test sets: 4,560 abstract, 1,822 review, and 2,452 topic instances (Appendix A). No method is trained or tuned on these data. Models. We generate with three LLMs from different providers, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Grok-4.1Fast (non-reasoning), and GPT-5.4-nano, accessed through Azure AI Foundry. Every call uses the same client and settings: the system message You are helpful assistant. and the prompt as the user message; style extraction requests JSON output. response blocked by the providers content filter is kept as an empty output and scored as such. RANDOM-SAMPLES uses the same template, but with entries drawn at random from the users own history instead of the most relevant ones, which isolates the effect of retrieval. As in LongLaMP, profile abstracts are truncated to their first 750 words in all methods. All prompts are in Appendix G. Reference-based metrics. As LongLaMP does, we report ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004), and METEOR (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005), computed with the LongLaMP evaluation code and averaged over test instances. Baselines. NO PROFILE sends the task input alone (e.g., Generate an abstract for the title . . . using the following items: . . . ), with no samples and no added instruction. LONGLAMP formats the retrieved entries with LongLaMPs own prompt templates (Kumar et al., 2024) and appends the LLM judge. Reference-overlap metrics reward shared content but say little about style. We therefore also score outputs with an LLM judge, GPT5.4-nano with low reasoning effort. The judge sees the task, the full generated output, and the full reference, and rates the output from 1 to 5 on nine 4 criteria with anchored descriptions of the extremes. Style Fidelity (SF) is the mean of Lexical, Syntax, Tone, Discourse, and Format; Task Quality (TQ) is the mean of Coverage, Factuality, Fluency, and Length. Both use the reference as the anchor; SPREFINEs own scores in steps 34 use the same five style criteria but the samples as the anchor, so the method never sees the judges anchor. Because the judge is also one of our generators, it may favor GPT-generated text (Panickssery et al., 2024); we therefore compare methods only within generator.

sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: Reference-based metrics. Table 1 compares SPREFINE with the baselines. SP-REFINE scores highest in 25 of 27 generatortaskmetric comparisons. It is above NO PROFILE in all 27, so the gains come from using the users writing; LONGLAMP is above RANDOM-SAMPLES in all 27, so choosing the most relevant samples matters as well. Relative to LONGLAMP, which sees the same retrieved samples, SP-REFINE improves by 10.2% on average (14.9% with DeepSeek, 4.4% with Grok, 11.5% with GPT; Table 6). The largest gains are on METEOR for review writing: +35.8% with GPT (0.2559 vs. 0.1885) and +32.7% with DeepSeek (0.2806 vs. 0.2114). The two exceptions are METEOR on review and topic writing with Grok, where LONGLAMP is higher (0.2900 vs. 0.2744 and 0.2485 vs. 0.2360). LLM judge. Table 2 shows that SP-REFINE improves Style Fidelity over LONGLAMP in 8 of 9 generatortask settings, by 0.21 points on average, and over NO PROFILE in all 9. Its Task Quality is higher than LONGLAMPs in 7 settings, equal in 1, and lower in 1 (GPT abstracts, 3.59 vs. 3.67), so the style gains do not come at the expense of content. The exception on Style Fidelity is GPT on review writing (2.18 vs. 2.34), where Format scores are low for every method that sees the samples (7.2). Figure 1 breaks the scores down by criterion: with DeepSeek, SP-REFINEs gain over LONGLAMP spans all five style criteria and is largest for Format (+0.97); with Grok, it is largest on Syntax and Tone; with GPT, all differences are within 0.13.

sections.title: 6 What Does Style Extraction Capture?
sections.content: Aggregate scores do not show whether the extracted profile describes the user. Because π is built from the retrieved samples only, the users reference text for the instance is held out from extraction and can serve as check. Figure 3 annotates one reference abstract with the aspects of its profile (Grok-4.1-Fast); Figures 7 and 8 (Appendix D) do the same for review and Reddit post. The profile predicts concrete, checkable habits. Extracted from four other abstracts, the profile predicts the abstracts rhetorical order (problem, method, evaluation, results; O2), its transition In this paper (D1), the qualifiers accurate and novel (L4), passive evaluation sentence built on the exact phrase is carried out using (S2), comma-separated series (S5), superiority shown by comparison (two to ten times faster than eight other . . . techniques; O3), the single unbroken paragraph (F1F2), and the sentence length (25.5 words vs. 24 predicted; S1). For the reviewer, the profile recovers the sign-off [2008 hyperbolium dot com] verbatim as fingerprint (X2), the contrast-based evaluation against earlier versions of each song (O3), and even metaphor the profile quotes from an earlier review (nosing their way; the reference has nosed its way towards discos rhythms, P4). Users depart from their own profile. The abstracts author writes in the first person (we propose, we derive) although the profile, built from impersonal samples, says to avoid it (P3), and closes on applications rather than performance claim (D3). The reviewer omits the fractional star rating the profile lists as fingerprint, and the Reddit user gives suggestions inline rather than as numbered list (S5). Style varies across users documents, which bounds how closely any profilebased method can match one reference.

sections.title: 7.1 Variants
sections.content: Each ablation removes part of SP-REFINE (Figure 4). SP-INFER: implicit inference, no extraction or revision. SP-INFER is single call that receives the numbered samples and the task and is asked to identify the authors style silently, draft, check the draft against the samples, and return only the text (Appendix G). Its prompt names seven informal cues but does not use STYLEPRISM, and no profile is produced. SP-REFINE uses this same call to produce its first draft, so comparing the two measures what explicit extraction and profile-guided revision add.

sections.title: 7.3 Oracles and Reference-Free Controls
sections.content: To bound what refinement can achieve, we evaluate variants that use information unavailable at inference time (Table 7, Appendix E). ORACLE-REGEN gives reviser the samples, the SP-INFER output, and the reference; in one call it scores the output on nine criteria (style against the samples; coverage and length against the reference) and writes revision, told to match the references length but not to copy its phrases. ORACLE-REGEN+P starts from the SP-PROFILE output instead. ORACLE-SELECT keeps, per instance, the candidate that the referenceanchored judge scores highest among {SP-INFER, ORACLE-REGEN}, among the three drafts SPREFINE produces (y0, y1, y2), or among {SPPROFILE, ORACLE-REGEN+P}. The referencefree control SP-REGEN uses the ORACLE-REGEN prompt with the reference block, the length target, and the copy instruction removed (Algorithm 4). The reference, not the revision, drives the oracle gains. With the reference visible, ORACLEREGEN raises ROUGE-L over SP-INFER by 0.07 0.13 for DeepSeek and Grok but at most 0.016 for GPT, and ORACLE-REGEN+P reaches ROUGEL 0.490 on DeepSeek abstracts. Removing the reference (SP-REGEN, Table 8) leaves the same revision with ROUGE-L change of at most 0.014 and lower METEOR in 6 of 9 settings. The oracle outputs reuse the reference: for DeepSeek, 57% of ORACLE-REGEN abstracts share an 8-word span with the reference that appears in neither the input nor the users samples, compared with 13% for SP-INFER. SP-REFINEs intermediate drafts are not much better. Choosing the best of y0, y1, and y2 with the reference-anchored judge (ORACLESELECT(SP-REFINE)) changes ROUGE-L over SP-REFINE by at most 0.008 for DeepSeek and 0.006 for Grok and GPT. The returned draft is close to the best that SP-REFINE produces; larger gains require new information, such as the reference.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced STYLEPRISM, taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects, and SP-REFINE, which uses it to make style extraction an explicit step in personalized long-form generation: the model writes down the users style with quoted evidence, then drafts from the users samples and revises against that profile. SP-REFINE outperforms LongLaMPs retrieval-augmented baseline in 25 of 27 referencebased comparisons and improves judged style fidelity, and the extracted profiles predict concrete habits that users held-out texts bear out. Ablations show that the profile is useful as revision guidance but cannot replace the samples, and that single implicit-inference call comes close. Oracle and control experiments show that larger refinement gains require the reference itself. Next steps are removing sample-format artifacts from the prompts and deciding per user or generator whether to revise.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We evaluate only the user setting of LongLaMP and only English data. Our LONGLAMP baseline uses LongLaMPs prompt templates and retrieval but our generators and generation settings, so absolute numbers are not directly comparable to those of Kumar et al. (2024). ROUGE and METEOR measure overlap with single reference and cap8 ture style only indirectly. Our LLM judge is model, not human, and also one of our generators; its scores use the reference as an anchor, so Style Fidelity partly reflects content similarity. SPREFINEs self-scores use the same five style criteria as the judge, anchored on the samples rather than the reference, which may favor SP-REFINE on the judges style criteria. The annotation study examines individual instances and is illustrative. We study prompting with fixed retriever and = 4; other retrievers, values of k, and fine-tuning are not explored. Oracle controls use sample of test instances, and closed-model APIs may change over time.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Systems that imitate persons writing style can be misused to impersonate that person or to produce deceptive text attributed to them. Our methods operate only on users own past writing for the purpose of assisting that user, and we do not release models trained to imitate specific individuals. Explicit profiles make what is being imitated inspectable, but they also summarize persons habits, including signature phrases and sign-offs, and should be treated as personal data. Generated text can repeat sentences from users earlier documents and invent quantitative claims; deployed systems should check for both. We use the publicly released LongLaMP benchmark (Kumar et al., 2024) for research purposes only, consistent with its intended use; its Hugging Face release does not state license. The data are derived from public scientific abstracts, Amazon reviews, and Reddit posts and may contain personal information, which we do not redistribute; the user texts shown in our figures are taken from the public benchmark. Use of AI assistants. We used AI assistants (Claude) to help write and debug experiment and analysis code, to format tables and figures, and to draft and edit parts of the text. The authors designed the study, ran all experiments, checked every number against the experiment outputs, and take full responsibility for the content.
